claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by synchronization of the reduction kinetics of all metal precursors.
Simultaneous precursor reduction enables uniform nucleation.
Simultaneous precursor reduction promotes rapid atomic interdiffusion.
Uniform nucleation and rapid atomic interdiffusion result in a homogeneous alloy.
Asynchronous reduction leads to phase segregation.
Asynchronous reduction leads to suboptimal surface-atom exposure.
Pt, Pd, Ru, Ir, and Os precursor ions have distinct natural reduction potentials.
A controlled slow-release reducing agent can tune the precursor reduction kinetics.
Slow release of the reducing agent can synchronize reduction of the different metal precursors.
Synchronization of nucleation and consolidation directly mediates homogeneous atomic mixing and alloy formation.
Matched reduction kinetics cause all precursor species to convert to their metallic states simultaneously.
Synchronized nucleation promotes uniform atomic interdiffusion.
Uniform interdiffusion produces a single-phase high-entropy alloy.
Uniform interdiffusion produces nanoparticles with high surface-atom exposure.
Under asynchronous reduction, early-reduced species nucleate and grow before the other metals enter the particles.
Sequential entry of metals caused by asynchronous reduction produces phase-segregated, heterogeneous alloy structures.
Relative to the uncontrolled baseline, slow-release reduction will produce more uniform, single-phase nanoparticles with better-exposed surface atoms.
The uncontrolled-reduction baseline will exhibit elemental segregation or multiphase formation and less favorable catalytic surface characteristics.
The proposed mechanism applies to solution-based wet-chemical synthesis of noble-metal HEA nanoparticles when metal-ion reduction is the activated step.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to physical vapor deposition or high-energy mechanochemical synthesis because those routes do not rely on chemical reduction.
